newsitem.title: USA: U.S. analysts say forex market to test G7 resolve.
newsitem.headline: U.S. analysts say forex market to test G7 resolve.

text.p: The currency market will push the dollar higher and test the resolve of the Group of Seven nations (G7) which hinted at its weekend summit in Berlin that the dollar's rapid rise should end, analysts said on Monday.
"It would be quite unusual for the market to reverse direction just on the basis of jawboning," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan and Co Inc.

"The fundamentals have not changed. The real danger here is you will probably see the market try to test G7 resolve and we may get more out of them than expected," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.

"The G7 were trying to send a signal to the market that enough is enough," he added, referring to the dollar's 55 percent rise versus the yen and 23 percent gain against the mark since hitting post-World War II lows in the spring of 1995.

The most telling part of the official G7 statement on currencies, released on Saturday, said that the major currency misalignments noted in the G7's previous April 1995 communique "have been corrected".
Dealers said the statement lacked the force needed to intimidate market players and override economic fundamentals which bode well for a stronger dollar.
"The G7 statement will not go down as a watershed event in foreign exchange history," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Nor do I think that the risk of intervention is greater than it was a week ago. There are still two chances of intervention -- slim and none," he added.

Overall, analysts interpreted the G7 statement as an attempt to foster some short-term stability in exchange rates and, at best, delay the dollar's rise. But of more import was what the report lacked -- evidence of a concerted effort to weaken the dollar.

Intervention seemingly was not even a topic of discussion at the summit. Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the subject of intervention was not discussed, while British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said the G7 did not reach any agreement on concerted intervention.
Moreover, analysts do not expect policymakers in any major industrial countries to adjust monetary policy to support or weaken their domestic currency.
"Germany and Japan are not in the position to raise interest rates to defend the weakness of their currencies. Nor is the U.S. likely to cut rates to slow down the dollar's rise," Chandler said.
The most recent bout of economic data releases show the U.S. economy continues to outperform most of continental Europe and Japan.
In January, the United States created 271,000 jobs while Germany lost 500,000 jobs and unemployment there soared to a post-war record of 4.66 million jobless.

Meanwhile, the Japanese government reported on Monday a surprise 12.8 percent tumble in December orders for private machinery, depicting a weak manufacturing sector. The market on average had expected a 1.7 percent decline, experts said.

Leven said Japan, the country most vocal about the need for foreign exchange stability, has had little room to maneuver since it altered monetary policy in 1995 to aid the dollar off its post-war lows by weakening the yen.

"The Bank of Japan (BoJ) has painted itself into a corner from which there is no graceful exit," Leven said, adding the unstable Japanese banking sector precludes a rise in interest rates to bolster the yen.
"If the BoJ starts intervening and draining liquidity by intervention, the Japanese stock market, already in trouble, could take it on the chin," he said.
However, Japanese and German officials had cause to cheer on Monday when the U.S. unit languished below Friday's closing levels against the mark and yen.

"We have been seeking a stable foreign exchange market and have said that excessive fluctuations were undesirable, which was stated in the G7 statement. The currency rate today reflects that," Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said on Monday.
Also, the Bundesbank's Tietmeyer said on Monday: "Until now, we saw the markets reacted in an appropriate way. The message sent from Berlin seems to be understood by the markets."
Analysts said the dealers understood the message, but like teenagers, given an excuse, they may rebel.
